prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "PEPSICO INC" (ticker PEP), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PEP", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: PepsiCo, Inc.
result.industry: Packaged snacks, foods and non-alcoholic beverages
markets: Salty and savory snacks (Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos, Tostitos, Ruffles)
Carbonated soft drinks (Pepsi, Mountain Dew, 7UP outside the US)
Sports, energy and functional drinks (Gatorade, poppi, Rockstar outside the US, distribution of Celsius and Alani Nu)
Bottled water, tea, coffee and juice drinks (Aquafina, Lipton and Starbucks ready-to-drink joint ventures)
Dips and better-for-you snacks (Sabra, Siete, Bare, PopCorners)

mission.statement: Create more smiles with every sip and every bite, serving more consumers, more occasions, more touchpoints
mission.source: PepsiCo website, Mission and Vision page (pepsico.com/who-we-are/mission-and-vision)
mission.plain: Make snacks and drinks that people enjoy, and get them to more people in more places.

about.plain: PepsiCo makes famous chips and drinks, like Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos, Pepsi, Mountain Dew and Gatorade, plus Quaker oats. It sells them in more than 200 countries. Its trucks deliver snacks straight to store shelves, which helps it keep its bags in the best spots. About 58% of its sales come from food and 42% from drinks.
about.customers: Supermarkets, big-box stores like Walmart (about 14% of sales), convenience stores, restaurants and bottlers, who then sell to ordinary shoppers.
about.everyday: If you have grabbed a bag of Doritos at a gas station or a Gatorade after sports practice, you bought a PepsiCo product.

money.plain: Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Aquafina, poppi
Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos, Tostitos, Quaker, Sabra, Siete

money.part: International drink concentrate sold to bottlers
money.plain: Pepsi syrup and brands licensed to partner bottlers
poppi prebiotic soda, Siete grain-free tortilla chips, Alani Nu energy drinks it distributes

result.summary: PepsiCo has a real but narrowing advantage: a portfolio of category-leading brands (Lay's, Doritos, Gatorade, Pepsi) and a direct-store-delivery network in North America that rivals cannot easily match on scale. That advantage is strongest in salty snacks; in soft drinks it is a clear number two to Coca-Cola. Years of heavy price rises followed by falling volumes, a 2026 price cut of up to 15% on core snacks and falling operating margins show the moat is being tested by value-seeking shoppers and changing diets.

pricingPower.evidence: Effective net pricing added about 14 points in FY2022 with flat organic volume, but in FY2024 and FY2025 roughly 4 points of pricing came with about a 2% organic volume decline, and in February 2026 PepsiCo cut prices on Lay's, Doritos and Cheetos by as much as 15% to win back shoppers; by Q3 2026 pricing added about 3 points with organic volume up about 0.5 point, though North America beverage volume was still down 2%.

moats.evidence: Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi, Mountain Dew and Quaker are household names sold in more than 200 countries and territories, and the 10-K names them as key trademarks.
Shoppers can switch from Doritos to a private-label chip or from Pepsi to Coke at no cost, as the 2024-2025 volume declines after price rises showed.
A snack or soda does not become more valuable to one buyer because others buy it.

With $93.9 billion of FY2025 revenue and a company-owned direct-store-delivery system for Frito-Lay and much of its North American bottling, PepsiCo spreads manufacturing, distribution and advertising costs over far more volume than snack rivals like Utz or Campbell's.

Store shelf space and delivery routes are limited, and retailers name PepsiCo the No. 1 supplier in the Kantar PoweRanking for 2025, the 10th year in a row, which makes it hard for new brands to get comparable placement.
PepsiCo is the incumbent; it has had to buy upstarts such as poppi ($1.95 billion, 2025) and Siete ($1.2 billion, 2025) rather than having a model incumbents cannot copy.
PepsiCo has been named to the Gartner Supply Chain Top 25 every year from 2021 to 2025, reflecting decades of know-how in snack manufacturing and route-to-market execution.
Beyond its trademarks, PepsiCo has no exclusive raw material or technology; its distribution deals for Celsius and Alani Nu depend on partner agreements rather than ownership.

customers.evidence: Retailers rate PepsiCo highly (No. 1 supplier in the Kantar PoweRanking for 10 consecutive years through 2025, and it appears on the Axios Harris Poll 100 reputation list 2022-2025), but consumers pushed back on price: organic volume fell about 2% in both FY2024 and FY2025 and PBNA beverage volume was still down 3% year to date in Q3 2026.

talent.evidence: PepsiCo was on Forbes' World's Best Employers lists 2020-2023, America's Best Large Employers 2021-2024, Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies 2021-2025 and LinkedIn Top Companies (US) in 2026, and employed about 306,000 people at the end of 2025, but it is not seen as a magnet for top technical talent.

product.evidence: Lay's and Doritos are category-defining snacks and Gatorade leads sports drinks, but Pepsi trails Coca-Cola in colas (Pepsi had about 8.3% of US carbonated soft drink volume in 2023 versus 19.2% for the Coke trademark, per Beverage Digest data) and PepsiCo has had to buy newer brands like poppi to keep up with modern tastes.

competitors.note: Lower-priced chips and sodas that gained when PepsiCo raised prices

estimates.name: Private-label snacks and drinks (Walmart Great Value, Costco Kirkland and others)

marketShare.measure: sales volume share by brand (Beverage Digest data via The Wall Street Journal)

threats: Value-seeking shoppers and private label: after double-digit price rises in 2022-2023, organic volume fell about 2% in FY2024 and FY2025, forcing price cuts of up to 15% on core snacks in February 2026
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and a broad shift toward less sugar, salt and processed food could shrink demand for chips and sodas
Regulation of food dyes, ingredients, marketing to children, sugar taxes and plastic packaging, all cited as risks in the FY2025 10-K
Coca-Cola's lead in colas and fast-growing energy and functional drink brands (Monster, Red Bull, Celsius) taking share of the beverage aisle
Falling North America profitability: operating margin fell from 14.3% in FY2020 to 12.2% in FY2025 and 2026 core EPS guidance was cut to +2.5% to +3.5% in October 2026
Heavy reliance on Walmart (about 14% of FY2025 net revenue) and growing retailer bargaining power
Input-cost inflation and tariffs on commodities such as potatoes, corn, oils, sugar and aluminum
Activist pressure (Elliott's roughly $4 billion stake, September 2025) could push structural changes such as bottling changes or portfolio separation

ceo.name: Ramon Laguarta
ceo.background: Spanish business executive; MBA from ESADE and Master in International Management from Thunderbird; joined PepsiCo in 1996 from Chupa Chups, ran Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa 2015-2017 and was President before becoming CEO in 2018 and Chairman in 2019

c1.evidence: PepsiCo leads mature snack and soft-drink industries; FY2025 net revenue grew only 2.3% with organic volume down about 2%.

c2.evidence: Shoppers choose Lay's, Doritos and Gatorade for familiar taste and brand, backed by a direct-store-delivery network that keeps shelves full, which is hard to copy; but the 2024-2025 volume declines after price rises show the preference is not unconditional.

c3.evidence: Almost everyone knows Pepsi, Lay's and Doritos and Frito-Lay is the default leader in US salty snacks, but in colas Pepsi is a clear second to Coca-Cola (8.3% vs 19.2% of 2023 US soft-drink volume for the Coke trademark).

c4.evidence: The mission to 'create more smiles with every sip and every bite' and the pep+ sustainability agenda are emphasised, but they describe selling more snacks and drinks rather than solving an important problem, and recent strategy has been driven by margins and activist pressure.

c6.evidence: “Pepsi, Doritos, Coke's rival, sugary and salty” are the first words most people associate with the name; the impression is familiar and mostly positive for taste and fun, but mixed on health.

c7.evidence: Snacks and non-alcoholic drinks are huge global markets, but they grow at low single digits and face a health-driven headwind rather than a strong secular tailwind; PepsiCo guided only about 3% organic growth for 2026.

c8.evidence: PepsiCo is pushing into functional drinks (poppi prebiotic soda, Celsius and Alani Nu distribution), protein snacks (Doritos Protein) and international snack markets, but these are extensions of food and beverages, not big new industries.

m1.evidence: Laguarta has laid out a shift toward 'positive choices', functional beverages and an AI-enabled, more integrated operating model, but that is an incremental vision for a consumer-goods company.

m2.evidence: Laguarta is a career PepsiCo manager (joined 1996) rather than a founder, and the company's 2025-2026 changes on prices and SKUs came under pressure from activist Elliott.

m4.evidence: There is no strong public evidence either way on whether Laguarta leads in a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: PepsiCo regularly launches new products (Simply NKD Doritos and Cheetos without artificial colors, Doritos Protein, a prebiotic Pepsi cola), but much of its recent growth in new categories came from buying poppi and Siete rather than inventing them.

m6.evidence: Laguarta has a business background (ESADE MBA, Thunderbird master's) and came up through commercial and regional management, not engineering.

m7.evidence: PepsiCo has been named one of Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies for 20 consecutive years through 2026 and promotes its pep+ sustainability goals, but there is little sign his stewardship is aimed at something far bigger than profit.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Laguarta giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Laguarta has a low-key, corporate public profile and is not known for a distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $70.4 billion in FY2020 to $93.9 billion in FY2025, but operating margin fell from 14.3% to 12.2%, North American volumes declined, the stock hit a six-year low in October 2026 and 2026 core EPS guidance was cut.

m10.evidence: PepsiCo runs continuing productivity programs, cut nearly 20% of its US product range and is centralising work in global capability centers, but it is not known for a Bezos-style culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: PepsiCo's snacks and drinks are enjoyed by huge numbers of people in more than 200 countries, but they are treats and conveniences rather than products that greatly improve lives.

p2.evidence: Making chips and soft drinks at scale requires strong logistics and brand building but is not extremely hard technically or critically important to the world.

f2.evidence: Gross margin slipped from 54.8% in FY2020 to 54.1% in FY2025 and operating margin fell from 14.3% to 12.2%.

f3.evidence: At September 5, 2026 total debt was $51,881m against $11,163m of cash and short-term investments, about 4.3 times FY2025 operating cash flow of $12,087m, though shareholders' equity was positive at $22,487m.

f4.evidence: Operating profit rose from $10,080m (FY2020) to $11,498m (FY2025) and operating cash flow from $10,613m to $12,087m, but both peaked earlier (operating profit $12,887m in FY2024, cash flow $13,442m in FY2023) and then fell.

v1.evidence: Lay's and Doritos are the go-to chips for many shoppers and Gatorade leads sports drinks, but Pepsi is not clearly better than Coke, and cheaper private-label chips are close substitutes.

v2.evidence: PepsiCo was on Forbes' World's Best Employers lists 2020-2023, Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies 2021-2025 and LinkedIn's Top Companies (US) in 2026, but it is not usually counted among the very top employers.

c5.evidence: If PepsiCo vanished, fans of Doritos, Lay's, Gatorade and Quaker and many retailers that rely on its deliveries would miss it, but rivals could replace most of its products and its health impact is debated.
